section.title: Sing a New Song for His Marvels
section.sectionRationale: Closely echoing the exodus victory song and Isaiah's promises of salvation reaching the ends of the earth, this enthronement psalm summons voices, instruments, and all creation, sea, rivers, and mountains alike, to celebrate the LORD's saving victory and His coming to judge the world in righteousness.
section.thesis: Because the LORD's own right hand and holy arm have worked salvation seen by all the ends of the earth, all the earth, and even creation itself, is summoned to a new song of joyful, musical praise as He comes to judge the world in righteousness.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a new song for the LORD's saving victory made known to the nations, verses 1-3; a summons to loud, musical praise before the King, verses 4-6; and creation's joyful chorus as the LORD comes to judge the earth, verses 7-9.

units.label: He has done wonders
units.note: a new song for the Lord's saving victory

verses.text: A Psalm. Sing to the LORD a {{chadash|new}} song, for He has done wonders; His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory.
The LORD has proclaimed His salvation and revealed His righteousness to the nations.
He has remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

units.label: Make a joyful noise before the King
units.note: a summons to loud, musical praise

verses.text: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth, let your cry ring out, and sing praises!
Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, in melodious song with the harp.
With trumpets and the blast of the ram's horn shout for joy before the LORD, the King.

units.label: He comes to judge the earth

verses.text: Let the sea resound, and all that fills it, the world, and all who dwell in it.
Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy
before the LORD, for He comes to {{shaphat|judge}} the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.

chadash.gloss: New, fresh. A new song answers a new act of God's salvation; Revelation 5:9 and 14:3 picture the redeemed singing just such a new song before God's throne.

shaphat.gloss: To judge, govern, or vindicate. The LORD's coming to judge the earth is not merely dreaded punishment but longed-for justice, the same role the New Testament assigns to Christ at His return, Acts 17:31.

basic.context: This psalm calls for a new song because the LORD's own right hand and holy arm have worked a visible salvation, seen by all the ends of the earth. Voices, harps, trumpets, and even the sea, rivers, and mountains are summoned to celebrate His victory and His coming to judge the world in righteousness.
basic.hermeneutics: The specific historical deliverance behind the psalm is not named, it may recall the exodus, the conquest, or deliverance from exile, but the psalm applies its call to sing a fresh song to every fresh act of God's salvation, and ultimately to the greatest salvation of all in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: A chadash, new, song is called for because the LORD's arm has worked visible salvation, seen by all the ends of the earth. His coming is to shaphat, judge or govern rightly, the world, a judgment longed for as vindication of the oppressed rather than merely feared.
basic.typology: The 'new song' of verse 1 anticipates the new song sung by the redeemed before God's throne, Revelation 5:9 and 14:3; the LORD's 'right hand and holy arm' working salvation anticipates the outstretched, wounded arms of Christ on the cross, through whom salvation was finally and fully worked.
basic.christ: This psalm's picture of salvation worked by the LORD's own right hand and holy arm, made known to the nations and seen by the ends of the earth, is fulfilled when Simeon holds the infant Jesus and calls Him God's salvation, 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' Luke 2:30-32, and the psalm's coming Judge is identified with Christ, appointed by God to judge the living and the dead, Acts 10:42.
basic.god: God is the mighty Deliverer whose own strength, not human armies, works salvation, faithful to His covenant love toward Israel while revealing His righteousness to every nation, and the coming Judge whose righteous rule sets even creation itself singing for joy.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 15:6 celebrates the LORD's right hand glorious in power, the same image this psalm uses of salvation. Luke 2:30-32 shows Simeon naming the infant Jesus as God's salvation revealed to the nations. Revelation 5:9 and 14:3 picture the redeemed singing a new song. Acts 17:31 fixes a day when God will judge the world through the Man He has appointed.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's new song for salvation worked by the LORD's own arm, made known to every nation, and its hope of a coming righteous Judge, finds its full answer in Christ, God's salvation revealed to the Gentiles and the appointed Judge of the living and the dead.

context.literary:
Psalm 98 is built like a three panel hymn, and each panel widens the circle of those who sing. Verses 1 to 3 are sung by Israel about what the LORD has done, and the verbs are all in the past: He has done wonders, proclaimed, revealed, remembered. Verses 4 to 6 turn to a command with three imperatives in a row in verse 4, then instruments named in verses 5 and 6, and the singers are now all the earth. Verses 7 to 9 reach past people altogether to the sea, the rivers and the mountains, and the reason for their song is given in the last two lines, He comes to judge.

The psalm begins and ends on the LORD as actor. Verse 1 says His own right hand and holy arm gained the victory, and verse 9 says He will judge. Everything between is response. Notice how the audience grows while the reason stays the same: Israel hears of a victory, the nations see it, and finally creation itself is summoned to applaud the verdict that is coming.

The sound of the psalm is part of its meaning. The verb for the shout in verse 4 and the word for the ram's horn blast in verse 6 come from the vocabulary of Israel's festivals and of the battlefield, where a shout announced a king. Verse 6 is the only line that names a king outright, and it does so at the pivot of the psalm, 'before the LORD, the King.' The instruments move from the lyre and harp, which accompany song, to trumpets and the ram's horn, which announce a ruler. The worship is turning from a concert into an acclamation.

Psalm 98 is also a close sibling of Psalm 96, and reading them together is a lesson in how the Psalter reuses its own language. Both open with the same call to sing a new song, both have the sea resounding and all that fills it, and both close on the LORD coming to judge the earth with righteousness and equity or faithfulness. Psalm 96 is addressed to the nations as a mission, 'Declare His glory among the nations,' Psalm 96:3. Psalm 98 sounds as though the declaring has already succeeded and the nations have simply seen what was done, verses 2 and 3.
context.historical:
The psalm carries no author's name and no stated occasion, only the word 'psalm' in its heading. That leaves its setting to be read from its language, and its language is saturated with Israel's memory of its first great rescue. 'His right hand and holy arm' recalls the song at the sea, where 'Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power,' Exodus 15:6, and the claim that the LORD won the victory alone, with no help from an army, is the same claim Israel made about the crossing of the sea. A people who had sung that song for centuries would hear this psalm as the old song growing new words.

Yet the psalm shares even more with the second half of Isaiah, the great message of comfort to a people in or near exile. Isaiah 52:10 says 'The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations; all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God,' which is almost a word for word match with Psalm 98:3. Isaiah 42:10 calls for a new song from the ends of the earth, and Isaiah 55:12 and 44:23 have mountains breaking into song and trees clapping. For a community that had known the destruction of Jerusalem and the silence of exile, the claim that nations had seen the LORD's salvation was a reversal of their own shame. The nations had watched Israel fall and had concluded that Israel's God was defeated. The psalm insists the nations will yet see the opposite.

The setting of use was public worship. The instruments in verses 5 and 6 are the ones the Chronicler assigns to the Levitical musicians at the ark and at the temple. The trumpets were blown by the priests at the feasts and to mark the new moon, as Numbers 10:10 lays down, and 2 Chronicles 5:13 shows trumpets, singers and instruments sounding together at the dedication of Solomon's temple. A first hearer would have pictured a festival procession with the whole apparatus of the temple orchestra.

The mention of the sea is not random decoration. In Israel's world the sea stood for chaos and for the peoples who threatened it, and to hear the sea itself called to roar in praise was to hear the old enemy put to work on the LORD's side.
context.canonical:
This psalm is one of the most widely echoed in all of Scripture. Within the Psalter it forms a matched pair with Psalm 96, and the Chronicler lifts lines from Psalm 96 and other psalms into the song David commissions when the ark is brought to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 16:31 to 33, where the sea resounds, the fields exult and the LORD 'is coming to judge the earth.' The new song itself runs as a thread through the book: Psalm 33:3, Psalm 40:3, Psalm 96:1, Psalm 144:9 and Psalm 149:1, and then Isaiah 42:10. Each time the song is called new because God has done something new, whether rescuing one man from a pit, as in Psalm 40:3, or defeating a people's enemies.

The prophets feed the psalm and are fed by it. Isaiah 52:10 and 49:6, where the LORD makes His Servant a light to the nations so that salvation reaches the ends of the earth, belong to the same field of promise.

In the New Testament the psalm is taken up at the birth of Christ. Mary's song says God has helped His servant Israel, 'remembering to be merciful,' Luke 1:54, which is the remembered love of verse 3, and Zechariah's song speaks of salvation raised up in the house of David, Luke 1:68 to 73. Simeon takes the eyes-have-seen language of verse 3 and says his own eyes have seen God's salvation, Luke 2:30 to 32. Paul uses the same verse 3 idea when he says the righteousness of God has been revealed, Romans 1:16 to 17 and 3:21, and he strings together psalms and Isaiah to show that the Gentiles were always meant to glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:9 to 11. At Athens he closes on the very note of verse 9, that God has set a day to judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed, Acts 17:31.

The book of Revelation gives the last turn. The song of Moses and of the Lamb, Revelation 15:3 to 4, draws on the language of the exodus song and on psalms like this one, and the new song of Revelation 5:9 and 14:3 is finally sung to the Lamb. Christian worship has kept Psalm 98 alive, and Isaac Watts's hymn 'Joy to the World' is a free paraphrase of its second half, which is why an Advent song about the birth of a child is really about the coming of the Judge and King.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants three things from those who sing this psalm. First, that they understand their own story rightly: what the LORD did was not a private rescue of a small people but a public act, done 'in the sight of' the nations, verses 2 and 3. Israel's deliverances were never only for Israel. Second, that they sing as if it were new. The command in verse 1 is not to repeat the old hymn but to make a song equal to what has just happened, and the song is to be loud, instrumental and communal. Third, that they place their hope in a judgment that is good news. The psalm ends not with Israel's enemies crushed but with a world set right, 'with righteousness' and 'with equity,' verse 9. The word for equity is built on the idea of straightness or levelness, so the picture is of a world finally made level, where the crooked places are put right.

The psalm also means to shape how Israel thinks of the LORD's faithfulness. The order in verse 3 is deliberate: He has remembered His love and faithfulness to Israel, and then all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation. The nations see salvation because God kept a promise to Israel. The particular act of covenant faithfulness becomes the means by which the whole world comes to know God. That is how a first hearer was meant to understand the place of Israel in the plan of God: chosen, yet chosen for the sake of everyone.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what the LORD has done and commands a response. The descriptions in verses 1 to 3 are the ground and the commands in verses 4 to 9 are the application. That order matters. The imperatives are not a formula for working up feeling, because each is a response to an event already accomplished. Believers today are not asked to manufacture joy but to tell the truth about what God has done and to let the truth be loud.

A careful reader should notice what is not prescribed. The psalm names lyre, harp, trumpet and ram's horn, but it does not make any of them a rule for worship. Verse 5 speaks of the lyre and melodious song together, and the Psalter elsewhere names flutes, cymbals and strings, so the instruments are examples drawn from Israel's own temple, not a specification. The principle is that the best sound a people can make belongs to God.

The command that the sea, rivers and mountains sing is poetry, not a call for nature worship or a claim that rivers have hands. It describes the world as it will be when the King is acknowledged, a way of saying that the created order was made to respond to its Maker and will.

Finally, the last verse describes a coming judgment, not a present programme. Believers are not told to execute judgment on the world but to rejoice that the LORD will do it. That sits beside Paul's counsel to leave vengeance to God, and it frees people to work for justice without needing to be the final judge.

debates.question: Are the verbs of verses 1 to 3 about a victory already won, or is the psalm looking ahead to a victory still to come?

views.label: A deliverance already won
views.case: The verbs in verses 1 to 3 are in the perfect, He has done, proclaimed, revealed, remembered, and the ends of the earth 'have seen.' On this reading the psalm celebrates a specific, completed act such as the crossing of the sea or the return from exile, and the coming judgment of verse 9 is the next step in the same story.

views.label: A prophetic perfect, speaking of the future as done
views.case: Hebrew poets sometimes use past verbs for what is so certain that it can be spoken of as accomplished. Because the nations in verses 2 and 3 had not all seen the salvation of Israel's God in any single historical event, some read the whole psalm as sung in the confidence of a victory God has already decided and will soon reveal.

views.label: A liturgical present that holds both
views.case: Because Israel sang the psalm repeatedly at its festivals, the perfect tense would serve each generation: a hymn recalling past saving acts so that the worshipper could sing of the LORD as a God who acts and who will act again.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the psalm grounds joy in what God has already done and places hope in what He has promised. The New Testament holds both moments together: the salvation has been revealed in Christ, Titus 2:11, and the judgment is still awaited, Acts 17:31.

debates.question: Is the coming of the LORD to judge in verse 9 a cause of fear or of joy?

views.label: Joy for the oppressed
views.case: The surrounding verses show the sea, rivers and mountains singing because He comes. The Hebrew idea of judging includes putting right, rescuing the wronged, and ruling, so judgment is good news where the world has been ruled by the strong, as in Psalm 72:1 to 4.

views.label: Joy and fear together
views.case: Because the judge is perfectly righteous, the same arrival that vindicates the faithful exposes the wicked. Psalm 96:9 calls the whole earth to tremble before Him in the same sequence, and Paul can say that God will judge the world, Acts 17:31, in a speech that calls people to repent.

debates.bearing: The psalm invites gladness at the coming Judge, but it does not hide that His righteousness takes evil seriously. For the believer the question becomes who stands as Judge, and the New Testament answers that the Judge is the One who died for sinners.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words and constructions repay a slower look.

First, the verb in verse 1 that the BSB renders 'gained Him the victory' is from the root yasha, the same root that gives 'salvation' in verses 2 and 3, yeshua. The translation rightly chooses 'victory' for the first, because the context is one of arms and battle, but the English loses the fact that the psalm is saying one thing three times: the LORD has saved, the LORD has made His salvation known, and the nations have seen the salvation of our God. The name Yeshua, Jesus, is built on the same root, and when Simeon says 'my eyes have seen Your salvation,' Luke 2:30, the ear that knows the Hebrew hears the name of the child in his arms. The word for 'arm,' zeroa, is what the exodus story and Isaiah both use for God's strength at work in history, as in Isaiah 52:10 and Exodus 15:16.

Second, verse 4 piles up commands, each a different word for noise. The first, 'make a joyful noise,' is from the root rua, to raise a shout, a word used of battle cries and of acclaiming a king, and the related noun teruah names the sound of the trumpet blast at the feasts in Numbers 10:10. The second, 'break forth,' has the sense of bursting open, the third is a word for a ringing cry, and the fourth, 'sing praises,' is the ordinary verb for making music. The sum is not politeness but volume. Verse 6 adds the ram's horn, shofar, which was the instrument that announced the new moon and the year of jubilee, and so it carried the sense of a proclamation that changes things.

Third, the word for 'equity' in verse 9, meysharim, belongs to the family of yashar, 'straight, level, upright.' The LORD judges the peoples 'with equity' in the sense of making rough places smooth and crooked things straight, a judgment that levels rather than merely punishes. It is the same word Psalm 96:10 uses of the judgment of the peoples, and Psalm 99:4 says of the King, 'You have established equity,' with the same word. The verb 'judge,' shaphat, in the ancient world covered governing as well as deciding cases, which is why the psalm can set it beside joy.

Fourth, the pair in verse 3, 'love and faithfulness,' chesed and emunah, are the two words that describe God's steadfastness to His covenant in Exodus 34:6, where He is 'abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' The BSB renders chesed here as 'love' and elsewhere as 'loving devotion,' so the reader may miss that the same pair is at work. And the verb 'remembered,' zakar, in Hebrew does not mean the recalling of a forgotten thing but acting on a commitment. When God remembers, He moves, as in Exodus 2:24 and Luke 1:54.

Finally, in verse 8 the rivers 'clap their hands,' which is a vivid image. The psalm does not simply say the rivers are glad; it gives them hands.

typology.type: The LORD's bared arm and the victory of the cross, verse 1 and verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 52:10 says the LORD 'has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations,' and the very next chapter, Isaiah 53:1, asks to whom the arm of the LORD has been revealed, before describing the Servant who was pierced. The pattern is of God's strength working through what looks like weakness. In Christ the arm is stretched out on the cross and the victory is a death, and Paul can say He disarmed the powers there, Colossians 2:15. The type falls short in one way: in the psalm the victory is seen at once by the watching world, while at the cross it was hidden from most until the resurrection, Acts 17:31.

typology.type: Israel's remembered covenant opening to the nations, verses 2 and 3
typology.fulfillment: The psalm moves from 'the house of Israel' to 'all the ends of the earth.' Luke 1:54 to 55 has Mary echo verse 3 as she says God has remembered mercy to Abraham and his offspring, and the offspring turns out to be the child in her womb. Paul sees the same movement in Christ, in whom Gentiles are brought near and the dividing wall is torn down, Ephesians 2:13 to 19, and quotes 'Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people,' Romans 15:10. The type falls short because the psalm pictures nations seeing Israel's salvation from outside, whereas in Christ they are made fellow citizens and part of the one body.

The call for a 'new song' is repeated through the Psalter, and in the book of Revelation it becomes the actual song of the redeemed: 'Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain,' Revelation 5:9. The Lamb is the reason for the new song, and the singers are drawn 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' the very nations of Psalm 98:2 and 3. Revelation 14:3 adds that only the redeemed could learn it. The type falls short in that the psalm's song is raised by anyone who has seen the LORD act, while the song of Revelation is learned only by those whose redemption the Lamb has purchased.

typology.type: The coming Judge who sets the world right, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's last line looks to the LORD who 'comes to judge the earth.' In the New Testament that coming is the return of Christ, who will sit on His glorious throne and gather all the nations, Matthew 25:31 to 32. Paul at Athens says God will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed, Acts 17:31, and Revelation pictures the rider called Faithful and True who 'with righteousness' judges, Revelation 19:11. The type falls short only in this: the psalm sees the judge coming, while the gospel shows that the Judge has already come once, to bear judgment in the place of those He will then welcome.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ in four ways, and the basic level has named only the first two.

It leads by the arm of the LORD. Isaiah, whose language this psalm shares, gives the arm a person. After 'The LORD has bared His holy arm,' Isaiah 52:10, the prophet asks, 'Who has believed our message, and to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' Isaiah 53:1, and the answer is the suffering Servant who bears our griefs. John sees Jesus fulfil this at the cross and in the signs before it, John 12:37 to 41. The same arm that shattered the enemy at the sea, Exodus 15:6, is the arm that was nailed open, and the victory is of the same kind: God's own doing, with no human help. Isaiah 59:16 says of the LORD that 'His own arm brought salvation,' because He saw that there was no one to intercede. In Christ He becomes the intercessor Himself, Hebrews 7:25.

It leads by the revelation of righteousness. Verse 2 says the LORD revealed His righteousness to the nations, and Paul picks the verb up to describe the gospel: 'For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith,' Romans 1:17, and 'now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed,' Romans 3:21. God's righteousness in the psalm is His saving faithfulness, and at the cross it is shown in the fullest way, because He is 'just and the one who justifies,' Romans 3:26. The nations to whom it is revealed are the Gentiles who now hear it, Romans 1:5.

It leads by the remembered promise. The verse that says He has remembered His love to the house of Israel is taken up in Mary's and Zechariah's songs, Luke 1:54 to 55 and 1:72 to 73, where the mercy promised to Abraham is being given in the child. The psalm's 'all the ends of the earth have seen' becomes literal when Simeon holds Jesus and speaks of a light for revelation to the Gentiles, Luke 2:30 to 32, and when Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth,' Acts 13:47.

And it leads by the coming Judge. The psalm's last verse is the Bible's gladdest view of judgment, and it is Christ who fills the role. The Father 'has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31, and the proof given is the resurrection. Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22. To the world, that could sound terrible, but the Judge is the One who was judged in our place. Believers sing the psalm with their eyes on a face.

A caution: the psalm does not mention a Messiah, and it is best not to force every line into a prophecy of Jesus. It is the psalm's own themes, the arm of God saving, righteousness revealed to the nations, love remembered and a righteous judge coming, that the New Testament says are brought to their peak in Him.
study.god:
Psalm 98 shows a God whose power and whose love are not in competition. The first verse says His own right hand and arm gained the victory, which is the language of unassisted strength: He does not need allies. Yet the third verse says the thing He remembered was love and faithfulness. The power is put in the service of a promise. A God who was only strong might terrify the world; a God who was only loving might be unable to rescue it. Here the two are one act.

The psalm also shows God as a King whose rule is worldwide but personal. He is called 'the King' only once, at the heart of verse 6, but every other line assumes it: He proclaims, reveals, remembers and judges, which are a king's actions. The psalm requires that the nations see this. God's kingship is not a national secret. It is a public fact that makes the sea and the mountains glad, and so the psalm gives one of the plainest answers in the Psalter to the question of whether Israel's God is only Israel's.

Third, it shows a God whose judgment is gladness. The last verse does not say He will judge 'with terror' but 'with righteousness' and 'with equity.' This tells us something about the doctrine of God: holiness and justice are not a threat hanging over the world but the thing the world was made to be ruled by. Creation is not afraid of the coming Judge. The created order sings because it has been waiting. Paul says as much when he speaks of creation groaning in eager expectation for its liberation, Romans 8:19 to 22.

The psalm also holds a tension. God's salvation has already been seen by all the ends of the earth, yet He is still coming to judge. The salvation is complete in its accomplishing, and the world is not yet fully set right. The God of the psalm is patient in a way that gives time for the nations to see and respond. Nothing in the text says the nations have all believed. It says they have seen.

What does this mean for worship? It means praise is the right response of the creature to God's action, not an optional extra. The psalm asks for every resource: voice, strings, brass, horn, the whole world. It asks for newness, because God's acts are not stale, and for loudness, because His victory was public. It also asks for gladness that is fitted to the facts. A people who had only a private rescue might sing quietly. A people who have seen the arm of the LORD reach the ends of the earth will not. And the psalm teaches that the hope of judgment, rightly understood, belongs in the congregation's song, not only in its fear.

crossReferences.note: The song at the sea says the LORD's right hand 'has shattered the enemy.' Psalm 98:1 borrows the image of the right hand and adds the holy arm, so that Israel's newest song is built on its oldest. The victory that freed the slaves is the pattern for every later salvation the psalm celebrates.

Almost the same line as Psalm 98:3: the LORD bares His holy arm and all the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God. The prophet places it at the end of a call for Zion to awake, immediately before the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, which tells the reader how the arm is revealed.

The sister psalm opens with the same new song and sends the singers out to declare His glory among the nations. Psalm 96 is the command to tell; Psalm 98 sounds like the report that the telling has been heard, so the two belong together as mission and celebration.

In David's song at the bringing in of the ark the sea resounds, the fields exult and the trees sing 'for He is coming to judge the earth.' The same closing line as Psalm 98:9 shows that the hope of the coming Judge was already part of the worship of the tent of the ark.

The prophet calls for a new song 'from the ends of the earth' from those who go down to the sea. Psalm 98:1 and 7 pick up both the new song and the sea, and the prophet makes explicit what the psalm implies, that the people best placed to sing are far from Jerusalem.

The mountains and hills burst into song and the trees of the field clap their hands as God's people go out with joy. Psalm 98:8 gives hands to the rivers, and both texts imagine nature joining in when the LORD's people are brought home, which fits the exile setting many see behind the psalm.

Mary sings that God has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful, as He promised to Abraham. This is the remembered love of Psalm 98:3 brought to its point: the child she carries is the means by which the remembered promise reaches its goal.

Simeon's 'my eyes have seen Your salvation' picks up the seeing of Psalm 98:3. He says the salvation is prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to Israel, which is exactly the order of the psalm, nations first seeing and Israel's glory retained.

Paul says the gospel reveals the righteousness of God, taking the word of Psalm 98:2 and naming the means. The righteousness revealed to the nations in the psalm is revealed in the gospel, 'to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.'

The redeemed sing a new song to the Lamb, drawn from every tribe, tongue, people and nation. Psalm 98 calls the nations to sing because God has acted; Revelation shows the singers gathered and gives the reason, the Lamb who was slain and purchased them for God.

Paul closes his speech to the Athenians by saying God has fixed a day to judge the world with justice by the Man He appointed. This is Psalm 98:9 applied: the Judge who comes is a man, and His resurrection is God's proof to everyone.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 98 sits in the middle of the story of the Bible and sings toward both ends of it.

It answers something from the beginning. Genesis opens with a world made to be ruled by God through people, and with a human family scattered at Babel into nations. The call to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, and the long years of Israel's history seemed to keep that promise narrow. The psalm is one of the places where the blessing is pictured as reaching the nations: they see salvation, they are told to shout, and the righteousness of God is revealed to them. Yet the psalm also answers something more basic. The sea, rivers and mountains sing because creation was made to praise its Maker, and the fall, which brought futility and bondage to creation, has kept the song from being sung as it was meant. The psalm pictures that song restored.

It sets up what comes after. The Old Testament pulls the thread through the exodus, the return from exile and the promises of a coming King and Servant, and every time a rescue is given the psalm's call to a new song is renewed. Isaiah takes the psalm's language and ties it to a Servant who is pierced, which tells the reader that the arm of the LORD will do its greatest work by suffering. The Gospels open with songs that reuse the psalm's words, because the long-remembered promise is arriving in a child. The apostles then carry the news to the ends of the earth, exactly as the psalm imagines, Acts 13:47.

It is not yet complete, and the psalm knows it, because it ends on the verb 'comes.' The story between the first coming and the last is the time in which the church sings, tells and waits. The new song has been given, but the judgment has not been delivered, and creation still groans, Romans 8:22.

The story ends where the psalm points. In Revelation the new song is sung before the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 5:9, the song of Moses and the Lamb is sung by those who conquered, Revelation 15:3 to 4, and a great multitude cries that 'the Lord our God the Almighty reigns,' Revelation 19:6. Then the Judge comes with righteousness, and what the psalm called equity, a world made level, is finally real. Nothing unclean enters the city, Revelation 21:27, and the sea and mountains no longer need to be summoned, because the whole creation is, at last, praising together. The psalm's reader can sing it now as a preview.

quiz.q: What has caused the LORD to be praised with a new song in verses 1-3?

options.text: His right hand and holy arm have worked a visible salvation, seen by all the ends of the earth.
options.note: Verses 1-3 credit God's own arm with a salvation made known to the nations and seen by the whole earth.

options.text: A new king has just been crowned in Jerusalem.
options.note: The psalm credits the LORD's own salvation, not a human coronation, as the cause for the new song.

options.text: The temple has just been rebuilt from its foundations.
options.note: Temple rebuilding is not the stated cause; the psalm specifically credits God's own saving action.

options.text: A new harvest has produced record grain yields.
options.note: The psalm's praise is for salvation and righteousness revealed, not agricultural abundance.

quiz.q: What instruments does the psalm name for musical praise in verses 5-6?

options.text: The lyre, the harp, trumpets, and the ram's horn.
options.note: Verses 5-6 specifically name the lyre, harp, trumpets, and ram's horn as instruments of praise.

options.text: Only hand clapping, with no instruments at all.
options.note: Rivers 'clap their hands' later as a poetic image, but verses 5-6 specifically name stringed and wind instruments.

options.text: Drums and cymbals exclusively.
options.note: The psalm names the lyre, harp, trumpets, and ram's horn, not drums and cymbals.

options.text: Bells worn on the priests' garments.
options.note: Priestly bells are not mentioned here; the named instruments are the lyre, harp, trumpets, and ram's horn.

quiz.q: How does creation respond in verses 7-8?

options.text: The sea resounds, the rivers clap their hands, and the mountains sing together for joy.
options.note: These verses personify the sea, rivers, and mountains joining in joyful praise before the LORD.

options.text: Creation falls completely silent in fear.
options.note: The psalm describes creation resounding and singing for joy, not falling silent.

options.text: Only human worshipers respond; creation is unaffected.
options.note: The psalm explicitly personifies the sea, rivers, and mountains as responding, not only human worshipers.

options.text: The mountains crumble in judgment.
options.note: The mountains are pictured singing for joy, not crumbling in judgment, in this psalm.

quiz.q: Why does the psalm say creation rejoices in verse 9?

options.text: Because the LORD comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with equity.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly grounds creation's joy in the LORD's coming righteous and equitable judgment.

options.text: Because a military alliance has been formed among the nations.
options.note: The stated reason is the LORD's righteous judgment, not any human political alliance.

options.text: Because the psalmist has composed a technically skillful poem.
options.note: The joy is grounded in God's coming righteous judgment, not the psalmist's poetic skill.

options.text: Because the harvest festival has concluded successfully.
options.note: The text specifically credits the LORD's coming judgment as the reason for creation's joy, not a festival's conclusion.

quiz.q: Who does the New Testament identify as fulfilling this psalm's hope that the ends of the earth would see God's salvation?

options.text: Jesus Christ, whom Simeon calls God's salvation and a light for revelation to the Gentiles.
options.note: Luke 2:30-32 records Simeon applying language like this psalm's directly to the infant Jesus.

options.text: The Roman Empire's expansion across the known world.
options.note: The New Testament identifies Christ, not any human empire, as the fulfillment of this hope.

options.text: The prophet Isaiah alone, with no further New Testament fulfillment.
options.note: Isaiah's prophecies anticipate this salvation, but Luke shows its fulfillment in the person of Jesus.

options.text: King Solomon's temple building projects.
options.note: Solomon's temple is not identified in the New Testament as the fulfillment of this psalm's hope for global salvation.

questions: The psalm calls for a 'new song' because of a fresh, visible act of God's salvation. What specific thing has God done for you recently that deserves its own fresh song of praise, rather than routine words?

This psalm envisions loud, full-voiced, instrumental praise, not quiet or restrained worship. Where might you be holding back in expressing joy and gratitude to God that this psalm would call you to release?
Even the sea, rivers, and mountains are pictured joining the praise. How does remembering that all creation is designed to glorify God shape the way you notice the world around you this week?

This psalm's hope, that the ends of the earth would see God's salvation, is fulfilled in Christ, revealed to the Gentiles. Who in your life still needs to hear and see that salvation made known through you?

Creation rejoices specifically because the LORD is coming to judge the world in righteousness and equity. Where in your life or in the world around you do you most need to trust that God's righteous judgment is still coming?

translationNotes.note: The phrase 'His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory' closely echoes the exodus song, 'Your right hand, O LORD, is glorious in power,' Exodus 15:6.
The 'ram's horn' translates the Hebrew shophar, a curved trumpet used both in worship and to announce significant events such as the Year of Jubilee.
The psalm's closing hope that the LORD will 'judge the world with righteousness' is echoed almost verbatim at the close of Psalm 96:13, forming a refrain across this cluster of enthronement psalms.
